title: A rope remembers its twist.
subtitle: Press. Set. Lift. Read what stays behind.
summary: A twisted rope touches workable material. Its strands leave a different surface from a smooth cord: a repeating pattern inside the groove.
sceneDescription: A three-strand rope lifted above a pale stone specimen, revealing a curved groove with repeated strand impressions.
modelNote: An invented contact experiment, not a reconstruction of an identified ancient mark. The surface approximates the negative of the modeled strands, with slightly smoothed edges; depth and timing are illustrative. It does not simulate material flow or rope deformation.

control.label: Use a twisted rope
control.offText: Smooth-cord comparison: the broad groove remains, but the repeating strand impressions disappear.

steps.name: Prepare
steps.title: A surface that can still yield.
steps.text: Begin with a workable specimen and a rope laid above it. The curved route is chosen for this experiment; it is not a tracing of an archaeological feature.

steps.name: Press
steps.title: Each strand makes contact.
steps.text: The rope sinks partway into the surface. A twisted rope has alternating low points, so contact can leave more information than the outline of a single groove.

steps.name: Hold
steps.title: Let the contact shape persist.
steps.text: For a sharp impression to survive, the material must retain detail as it sets. A real trial would vary consistency, pressure, fiber type, and the time before removal.

steps.name: Lift
steps.title: Take the rope away.
steps.text: The rope lifts from the specimen. The negative of its lower strands remains in the model. Sticking, smearing, and damage on release would have to be measured in a physical trial.

steps.name: Read
steps.title: Look inside the groove.
steps.text: Compare the twisted rope with the smooth cord. Repeated oblique impressions could be more informative than a rope-like curve alone. Their origin and age would still need investigation.

issues.title: A curved mark in hard stone
issues.mechanism: Contact before hardening can transfer a curved shape without carving that curve into already hard material.
issues.remaining: Later rope abrasion, tool marks, weathering, and impressions in a younger coating can also produce surface features.

issues.title: Fine detail inside a groove
issues.mechanism: A yielding surface could copy the rope's strand spacing and direction of twist.
issues.remaining: A candidate needs a measured surface profile and a documented archaeological context. This scene supplies neither an ancient example nor its date.

issues.title: Separating shape from process
issues.mechanism: Changing only the rope makes a simple comparison: a broad channel versus a channel with strand detail.
issues.remaining: Replicas and alternative processes must be compared under the same imaging conditions before a mark can diagnose its cause.

hypothesis: This atlas proposes a contact experiment: a rope could impress material that was workable at the time of contact. That could be a cast body, a surface layer, or a later repair; the impression alone does not distinguish them.
alternative: Compare an impression with a rope dragged across hard stone, deliberate tool grooves, and natural surface damage. A resemblance in a photograph is a starting point for measurement.
test: Press both smooth cord and twisted rope into a candidate mixture. Record pressure and release time; scan the cured surfaces. Compare them with abrasion controls and a measured ancient feature, including the direction and spacing of any strand detail.
